name: Infrastructure Automation Essentials
description: Domain adaptation of Platform Adoption Essentials for infrastructure automation and Infrastructure as Code (IaC) practices. Provides vendor-agnostic terminology mapping and extends the baseline with managed asset lifecycle and governance concerns.

focuses.name: Value

focuses.name: Solution

focuses.name: Endeavor
focuses.description: Governs the execution of the transformation, encompassing people, processes, and policies.

narrativeTypes.name: The STAR Format
narrativeTypes.description: Enforces a strict cause-and-effect relationship between context and outcomes (Situation, Task, Action, Result).

narrativeElements.name: Situation
narrativeElements.description: The context or background of the challenge.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the specific situation, context, or baseline state before action is taken.

narrativeElements.name: Task
narrativeElements.description: The specific challenge, objective, or requirement.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the specific task, problem, or goal that needs to be addressed.

narrativeElements.name: Action
narrativeElements.description: The specific steps or interventions performed.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the methodology, activities, or steps taken to address the task.

narrativeElements.name: Result
narrativeElements.description: The outcome, impact, or value achieved.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Summarize the measurable results, outcomes, or state changes achieved from the actions.

narrativeTypes.name: The Hero's Journey
narrativeTypes.description: Highly effective for macro-level lifecycle orchestrations (platform adoptions, transformations).

narrativeElements.name: The Ordinary World
narrativeElements.description: The starting point before the transformation.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the current, pre-platform state of the organization.

narrativeElements.name: The Call to Adventure
narrativeElements.description: The catalyst for change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the business opportunity, crisis, or driver that necessitates the platform transformation.

narrativeElements.name: The Ordeal
narrativeElements.description: The core transformation challenges and execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the complex adoption activities, migrations, and challenges faced during implementation.

narrativeElements.name: The Return
narrativeElements.description: The new operational baseline and realized value.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the successful adoption, the accrual of benefits, and the new optimized way of working.

narrativeTypes.name: The Three-Act Structure & StoryBrand
narrativeTypes.description: Positions the consumer as the Hero and the Platform Engineering team as the Guide utilizing the defined approach.

narrativeElements.name: Act I: The Hero and the Problem
narrativeElements.description: Identifying the consumer and their pain points.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Identify the primary consumer (the Hero) and detail the specific friction or problem they face.

narrativeElements.name: Act II: The Guide and the Plan
narrativeElements.description: The platform team offers a solution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the Platform Engineering team as the Guide who provides a clear, paved-path approach or plan.

narrativeElements.name: Act III: Call to Action and Success
narrativeElements.description: Execution and outcome.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the call to action for the consumer to adopt the plan, and the successful outcome of doing so.

narrativeTypes.name: Micro-Narratives (ABT)
narrativeTypes.description: Shorter frameworks (And/But/Therefore) designed for rapid, highly persuasive daily execution updates.

narrativeElements.name: And (Context)
narrativeElements.description: The current situation and baseline facts.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the current agreed-upon context, background, and baseline facts.

narrativeElements.name: But (Conflict)
narrativeElements.description: The problem, challenge, or contradiction.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the specific problem, blocker, challenge, or contradiction encountered.

narrativeElements.name: Therefore (Resolution)
narrativeElements.description: The action taken or conclusion reached.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the specific action taken, decision made, or conclusion reached to resolve the conflict.

narrativeTypes.name: User story
narrativeTypes.description: A brief, informal explanation of a software feature written from the perspective of the end user.

narrativeElements.name: As a [role]
narrativeElements.description: This identifies the specific persona or role interacting with the feature.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define constraints. Instead of saying "user," say "First-time Visitor" or "System Administrator." This helps the developers understand if the UI should be "idiot-proof" or "power-user focused."

narrativeElements.name: I want to [perform some action]
narrativeElements.description: This is the intent or the feature itself. It describes the action the user wants to take within the software.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Keep this focused on the what, not the how. Avoid mentioning specific UI elements. Focus on the functional capability you are giving them.

narrativeElements.name: So that [I can achieve some goal]
narrativeElements.description: This is the purpose. It explains the underlying problem the user is trying to solve or the value they hope to gain.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the work. If you cannot find a compelling So that statement, the feature might not be worth building. It also helps developers suggest better technical solutions if they understand the ultimate goal.

narrativeTypes.name: Epic
narrativeTypes.description: A well-structured Epic provides a north star for the team, ensuring everyone knows why a large project exists and what success looks like.

narrativeElements.name: Summary
narrativeElements.description: A clear, punchy title and a one-sentence elevator pitch that describes the high-level initiative.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Treat this as the project's identity. Use it in stakeholder meetings and roadmap views to provide an instant understanding of what is being built without getting bogged down in details.

narrativeElements.name: Strategic Intent
narrativeElements.description: This section explains how this Epic aligns with the company's broader business goals or quarterly objectives (OKRs).
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the budget and resource allocation. If you can't link the Epic back to a specific business value, it shouldn't be an Epic.

narrativeElements.name: User Personas
narrativeElements.description: A list of the primary and secondary users who will be impacted by this large-scale change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to keep the scope focused. When brainstorming features, ask: Does this specific feature serve the personas listed in the Epic? If not, it belongs in a different Epic.

narrativeElements.name: High-Level Requirements
narrativeElements.description: These are not detailed stories yet, but rather the broad capabilities the system must have once the Epic is finished.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use these as themes to help you brainstorm the individual User Stories later. They serve as the framework for your backlog.

narrativeElements.name: Success Metrics
narrativeElements.description: The quantitative data points that will prove the Epic was a success after it is released.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define the Definition of Done for the entire project. Instead of saying when the code is finished, use when the checkout conversion rate hits 5%.

narrativeTypes.name: Lifecycle
narrativeTypes.description: A standard lifecycle orchestration framework to map progression phases.

narrativeElements.name: Prerequisites
narrativeElements.description: Conditions required before starting the lifecycle.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Define the Phase 0 or preparation steps, including baseline checks or prerequisite states, that must be achieved before the main lifecycle begins.

narrativeElements.name: Lifecycle Phase
narrativeElements.description: An active stage of lifecycle execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the active state transitions, required work products, and activities for this specific phase of the lifecycle progression.

narrativeTypes.name: Essay Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A cohesive narrative format that guides the reader carefully through the evidence for and against a proposition before reaching a conclusion.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: The start of the essay used to contextualise the work and grab the attention of the reader.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Explain how the topic sits within the framework of the subject area as a whole. Outline the structure of your essay very briefly, but do not give your conclusions away on the first page.

narrativeElements.name: Defining Key Concepts
narrativeElements.description: A section establishing the interpretation of central concepts without relying on dictionary definitions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Relate in your own words how the terms you will be using are to be interpreted within the context of your essay.

narrativeElements.name: Presenting Evidence
narrativeElements.description: The core discussion where secondary works are evaluated and viewpoints are balanced against each other.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Be selective in your choice of evidence and use signposting language to guide your reader. Quote sparingly, paraphrase occasionally, and summarise often to integrate other people's ideas into your own argument.

narrativeElements.name: Conclusion
narrativeElements.description: The closing section that synthesises the presented evidence and forms a direct response to the assignment title.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Draw the threads of your argument together. Do not bring in new evidence in your concluding paragraphs or try to cram in ideas that you have not developed fully.

narrativeTypes.name: Report Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A formal, informative structure broken down into sections and sub-sections to order and communicate relevant information in an easily navigable way.

narrativeElements.name: Executive Summary
narrativeElements.description: A stand-alone summary of the entire report's purpose, methodology, findings, conclusions, and recommendations.
narrativeElements.howToUse: This should be the last thing that you write. Keep it concise (usually a paragraph or two and always less than a page) to enable the reader to make an informed decision about whether they want to read the report itself.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: Explains the rationale for undertaking the work reported on, the background, and the scope of the report.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State what the report is about, define how it meets the requirements of the brief, and explain your research methods.

narrativeElements.name: Methods
narrativeElements.description: A clear description of how the investigation was carried out and why specific methods were chosen.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Write this section concisely but thoroughly. Provide step-by-step details in such a way that a reader could replicate the research you have done.

narrativeElements.name: Results and Findings
narrativeElements.description: A purely factual presentation of the research data using text, graphs, tables, or diagrams.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Present the findings of your research as simply as possible. Save your interpretation of the results for the Discussion section.

narrativeElements.name: Discussion
narrativeElements.description: The section that brings everything together by showing how the findings relate to the purpose of the report and previous research.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Interpret the results, showing how they respond to the brief explained in the introduction. Mention if there were any problems or unexpected results and how they were solved.

narrativeElements.name: Recommendations
narrativeElements.description: Suggestions for a future course of action based on the evidence and conclusions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Make recommendations that solve problems or help to develop a new strategy. Make an effort to sound authoritative and certain in your choices.

narrativeTypes.name: SDLC
narrativeTypes.description: Software Development Lifecycle pattern for systematic technical delivery from requirements through maintenance.

narrativeElements.name: Plan
narrativeElements.description: Requirements gathering and project planning phase.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Define objectives, scope, requirements, and success criteria for the initiative.

narrativeElements.name: Design
narrativeElements.description: Architecture and detailed design phase.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Establish technical architecture, design patterns, and implementation approach.

narrativeElements.name: Build
narrativeElements.description: Implementation and construction phase.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Develop, configure, and assemble the solution components.

narrativeElements.name: Test
narrativeElements.description: Validation and quality assurance phase.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Verify functionality, performance, security, and integration through testing.

narrativeElements.name: Deploy
narrativeElements.description: Release and deployment phase.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Roll out to production environment with appropriate deployment strategy.

narrativeElements.name: Maintain
narrativeElements.description: Operations and continuous improvement phase.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Monitor, optimize, patch, and evolve the solution in production.

narrativeTypes.name: PDCA
narrativeTypes.description: Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle (Deming Cycle) for continuous improvement and iterative refinement.

narrativeElements.name: Plan
narrativeElements.description: Establish objectives and processes.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Identify improvement opportunity, analyze current state, and plan intervention.

narrativeElements.name: Do
narrativeElements.description: Implement the plan on small scale.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Execute the planned change or experiment in controlled environment.

narrativeElements.name: Check
narrativeElements.description: Measure and evaluate results.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Assess outcomes against objectives, identify gaps and learnings.

narrativeElements.name: Act
narrativeElements.description: Standardize or iterate based on learnings.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Scale successful changes, adjust plan based on findings, repeat cycle.

narrativeTypes.name: Build-Measure-Learn
narrativeTypes.description: Lean Startup cycle for validating assumptions through rapid experimentation and feedback.

narrativeElements.name: Build
narrativeElements.description: Create minimum viable solution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Develop smallest increment that can test key hypothesis or assumption.

narrativeElements.name: Measure
narrativeElements.description: Collect data and feedback.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Instrument, observe, and gather quantitative and qualitative evidence.

narrativeElements.name: Learn
narrativeElements.description: Analyze and decide next iteration.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Synthesize findings, validate or invalidate hypothesis, pivot or persevere.

narrativeTypes.name: Design-Build-Run-Optimize
narrativeTypes.description: Architectural lifecycle for infrastructure and platform engineering spanning conception through continuous improvement.

narrativeElements.name: Design
narrativeElements.description: Architecture definition and planning.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Define architecture, topology, technology choices, and capacity planning.

narrativeElements.name: Build
narrativeElements.description: Provisioning and configuration.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Deploy infrastructure, configure systems, establish integrations and connectivity.

narrativeElements.name: Run
narrativeElements.description: Operations and steady-state management.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Monitor health, respond to incidents, maintain availability and performance.

narrativeElements.name: Optimize
narrativeElements.description: Continuous improvement and evolution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Tune performance, reduce costs, enhance capabilities based on operational insights.

narrativeTypes.name: Crawl-Walk-Run
narrativeTypes.description: Maturity progression model for incremental capability building and adoption.

narrativeElements.name: Crawl
narrativeElements.description: Initial capability establishment.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Establish foundational capability with limited scope, manual processes, learning focus.

narrativeElements.name: Walk
narrativeElements.description: Capability refinement and scaling.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Expand scope, introduce automation, standardize processes, build confidence.

narrativeElements.name: Run
narrativeElements.description: Mature, optimized operation.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Full automation, enterprise scale, optimization focus, continuous evolution.

competencies.name: Analysis
competencies.description: The ability to understand infrastructure needs, assess automation tool options, make informed decisions about automation strategy, and conduct coverage gap analysis across the infrastructure estate.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands basic infrastructure automation needs and can parse user feedback about provisioning pain points.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can map simple infrastructure consumer requirements to existing automation capabilities and identify basic friction points in provisioning workflows.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently translate complex stakeholder needs into actionable automation requirements, conduct coverage gap analyses, and define the boundaries of the thinnest viable automation platform.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can analyze shifting enterprise infrastructure landscapes to identify new automation opportunities, evaluate multi-cloud strategies, and assess organizational readiness for advanced automation maturity.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Pioneers new analytical methods for infrastructure automation value stream mapping, IaC maturity assessment, and enterprise capability evaluation.

competencies.name: Engineering
competencies.description: The ability to design, build, and implement infrastructure automation solutions. Encompasses IaC authoring (HCL, YAML, Ruby DSL, Puppet DSL), module development, testing strategies (Terratest, Molecule, InSpec, Test Kitchen), CI/CD pipeline construction for infrastructure code, state management design, and multi-tool integration architecture.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands fundamental IaC concepts (desired state, idempotency, convergence) and can read basic automation code (playbooks, manifests, .tf files).

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can implement basic infrastructure automation using established modules and patterns. Can write simple playbooks, Terraform configurations, or manifests based on documented guidance.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently develop reusable modules, design automation workflows, and build CI/CD pipelines for infrastructure code. Understands state management, testing strategies, and multi-environment promotion.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can architect complex, multi-tool automation systems spanning multiple cloud providers. Resolves systemic integration challenges, designs module library architectures, and establishes organizational automation standards.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Develops novel automation paradigms, contributes to open-source automation tools, and shapes industry direction for infrastructure automation practices.

competencies.name: Leadership
competencies.description: The ability to inspire, guide, and motivate automation teams. Encompasses championing the cultural transformation from manual to automated operations, establishing psychological safety for complex automation efforts, and leading organizational change for IaC adoption.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Can participate effectively in automation team environments and support overarching automation goals.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can guide small automation squads and foster adherence to established IaC practices and coding standards.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can inspire automation teams to embrace IaC-first culture, champion blameless post-mortems for automation failures, and establish psychological safety for complex infrastructure changes.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can lead large-scale cultural transformations from manual to automated operations, overcoming deep organizational resistance to codified infrastructure and self-service models.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Acts as an industry-recognized visionary, shaping the global discourse on infrastructure automation culture, team design, and organizational transformation.

competencies.name: Management
competencies.description: The ability to plan, organize, and coordinate automation work. Encompasses delivery cycle management, capacity allocation, cross-functional coordination, IaC maturity roadmap management, and governance of automation initiatives.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands basic task tracking, automation work item management, and team coordination.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can manage the delivery of discrete automation capabilities and organize daily operational workflows for infrastructure code development.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently orchestrate cross-functional automation delivery cycles, balance technical debt against feature velocity, and manage automation platform service-level agreements.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can adapt delivery structures across highly matrixed environments, transitioning organizations from project-based to product-centric automation platform lifecycles.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Develops novel management and operational frameworks that redefine how enterprises deliver infrastructure automation services at scale.

competencies.name: Platform Security And Compliance Enforcement
competencies.description: The ability to design, implement, and automate security policies (OPA, Sentinel, Kyverno), access controls (RBAC, ABAC), and compliance checks (CIS, SOC 2, PCI-DSS) within the automation platform and managed infrastructure.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands basic IaC security principles (secrets management, state encryption) and compliance requirements (CIS benchmarks, regulatory frameworks).

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can configure basic security settings for automation platforms, implement access controls, and run security scanning tools based on documented procedures.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently design comprehensive security architectures for automation systems, author Policy-as-Code rules, and automate compliance auditing across infrastructure estates.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can adapt security strategies to address novel threats in multi-cloud automation environments, design graduated policy enforcement, and architect zero-trust automation pipelines.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Develops new paradigms for infrastructure automation security, proactive threat hunting in IaC code, and AI-driven compliance enforcement.

competencies.name: Platform Strategic Alignment
competencies.description: The ability to align automation capabilities and roadmap with broader business goals, economic models (FinOps), and enterprise architecture strategies. Encompasses connecting automation investment to business outcomes and ensuring the automation platform evolves with organizational needs.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands the high-level business drivers for infrastructure automation (cost reduction, compliance, speed).

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can articulate how specific automation capabilities support identified business opportunities and operational improvements.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can develop and manage automation platform roadmaps that demonstrably drive business value, ROI, and operational efficiency improvements.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can pivot automation strategy in response to shifting organizational needs, cloud provider changes, or regulatory landscape evolution.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Pioneers new automation business models, FinOps strategies, or economic frameworks that redefine enterprise infrastructure value.

competencies.name: Site Reliability
competencies.description: The ability to apply software engineering principles to infrastructure operations, ensuring automation system reliability, managed infrastructure availability, and operational performance. Encompasses drift detection and remediation, SLO design for managed infrastructure, incident response for automation failures, self-healing system design, and disaster recovery automation.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands basic monitoring concepts, SLIs/SLOs, and incident response procedures for automated infrastructure.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can implement monitoring and alerting for automation systems, participate in incident response, and execute drift remediation runbooks.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently design drift detection and remediation workflows, define SLOs for managed infrastructure, and lead complex incident resolutions involving automation failures.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can architect self-healing infrastructure systems, implement predictive maintenance, and establish enterprise-wide reliability practices for automated infrastructure estates.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Develops novel approaches to infrastructure reliability, autonomous remediation, or predictive infrastructure management.

competencies.name: Stakeholder Representation
competencies.description: The ability to gather, communicate, and balance the needs of infrastructure consumers (developers, SREs, security teams, operators) and accurately represent their views to the automation platform team.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands the different consumer personas utilizing the automation platform (developers, SREs, operators, security engineers).

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can effectively gather and advocate for the needs of a specific infrastructure consumer team.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can accurately balance competing requirements from security, networking, operations, and developer teams to ensure the automation interface remains frictionless and effective.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can negotiate complex political landscapes, aligning executive objectives with the daily operational realities of the infrastructure automation workforce.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Creates novel enterprise feedback loops and representation models that radically democratize automation platform evolution.

narratives.name: Managed Asset Lifecycle
narratives.description: Lifecycle narrative describing the progression of a managed infrastructure resource from discovery through decommissioning.

narrativeContexts.context: Before a managed asset can begin its lifecycle journey, the automation platform must be at least at the Provisioned state, with CI/CD pipelines operational and module registries accessible. Automation requirements must be at least at the Bounded state, defining which infrastructure resources are in scope for automation management. At least one automation artifact (module, role, cookbook) must be available for the resource type being managed.

The managed asset is discovered through cloud API enumeration, network scanning, or manual identification. Its desired state is formally declared in automation code (Terraform resource block, Ansible task, Puppet resource declaration). The automation code is peer-reviewed, tested, and applied to create the resource or import an existing resource into automation state management. Post-provisioning verification confirms the resource matches its declared configuration. This phase transitions the asset through Discovered, Defined, and Provisioned states.

The managed asset enters steady-state operation with monitoring, drift detection, and configuration enforcement active. SLI/SLO tracking ensures operational health. The asset adapts to demand through auto-scaling policies (for cloud-native resources) or capacity planning (for static resources). Drift deviations are detected and remediated through automated or guided workflows. This phase covers the Operational and Scaling states.

When the managed asset is no longer needed, it enters systematic retirement. Workloads are drained, dependencies updated in automation code, and the resource is destroyed through automation tools (terraform destroy, puppet node deactivate). State files are cleaned up, monitoring alerts suppressed, and cost tracking updated. Post-decommissioning verification confirms complete removal from all systems. This phase covers the Decommissioning state.

narratives.name: Asset Governance Maturity Progression
narratives.description: Crawl-Walk-Run narrative describing the organizational journey from unmanaged infrastructure to self-healing autonomous operations.

narrativeContexts.context: The organization begins with infrastructure in an Unmanaged state -- resources provisioned manually, no comprehensive inventory, shadow IT prevalent. The first step is achieving Inventoried status by deploying discovery tools, cataloging assets with metadata, assigning ownership, and quantifying the coverage gap. As the inventory matures, codification begins: infrastructure definitions are written, existing resources imported into state management, and IaC-first policies established. The organization progresses through Unmanaged, Inventoried, and Codified states.

With infrastructure codified, the focus shifts to convergence and governance. Drift detection runs on schedule across the estate, deviations are classified and remediated systematically, and the gap between declared and actual state is minimized. Policy-as-Code is deployed at portfolio scale with graduated enforcement. Compliance reporting becomes automated, generating audit evidence without manual effort. The organization progresses through Converged and Governed states.

At the highest maturity level, the infrastructure estate becomes self-sustaining. AI-driven anomaly detection identifies emerging problems proactively. Automated remediation resolves known failure patterns within defined operational boundaries (tiered: auto-fix for low-risk, auto-ticket for medium-risk, page-human for high-risk). Predictive maintenance anticipates failures before they occur. The organization achieves Self-Healing state -- zero-touch operations within operational guardrails.

narratives.name: Infrastructure Automation Maturity Journey
narratives.description: Baseline-level narrative describing the Infrastructure Automation Essentials maturity journey using a Crawl-Walk-Run progression.

narrativeContexts.context: The organization begins its infrastructure automation journey by establishing foundational capabilities. Manual infrastructure management pain points are documented and quantified. An automation toolchain is selected based on requirements (Terraform, Ansible, Puppet, Chef, or Salt). The first automation engineers are identified and trained. Initial automation code is authored for a pilot set of infrastructure resources, demonstrating the basic value of desired-state declaration, idempotency, and version-controlled infrastructure. The automation platform is provisioned with basic CI/CD pipelines and module registries. Early wins build organizational confidence and stakeholder buy-in. Asset Governance transitions from Unmanaged to Inventoried as discovery tools catalog existing infrastructure.

With foundational capabilities proven, the organization scales automation practices across teams and infrastructure domains. Reusable automation artifacts (modules, roles, cookbooks) are developed and published to internal registries. Self-service interfaces enable non-specialist infrastructure provisioning through golden path templates. Human error accounts for approximately 80% of IT outages, and the average cost of unplanned downtime exceeds $300,000 per hour. Only 13% of organizations report achieving IaC maturity, while 98% recognize the need for more IaC expertise.

Establish a comprehensive, vendor-agnostic framework for infrastructure automation that enables organizations to systematically transition from manual infrastructure management to automated, code-driven operations. The framework must address the complete automation lifecycle from tool selection through self-healing infrastructure, encompassing provisioning, configuration management, drift detection, policy enforcement, and autonomous remediation.

Infrastructure Automation Essentials adapts the Platform Adoption Essentials kernel for the IaC domain through alias-driven terminology mapping and targeted extensions. Eight PAK alphas are aliased to IaC-specific terms (e.g., Platform becomes Automation Platform, Platform Asset becomes Automation Artifact). Two new alphas -- Managed Asset and Asset Governance -- address the lifecycle of individual infrastructure resources and portfolio-level governance maturity respectively. Six new activity spaces provide the execution boundaries for the new concerns. The framework is tool-agnostic, supporting Terraform, Ansible, Puppet, Chef, Salt, and emerging tools through universal automation abstractions.

Organizations adopting Infrastructure Automation Essentials gain a structured framework for measuring and advancing their automation maturity. The progressive state models enable data-driven maturity assessment, targeted improvement planning, and quantifiable progress tracking. Extension practices built on this baseline can address specific tool implementations (e.g., Terraform-specific practices, Ansible-specific practices) while maintaining structural compatibility with the broader platform engineering ecosystem through the PAK foundation.

narrativeContexts.context: Infrastructure Automation Essentials synthesizes knowledge from the following authoritative sources spanning infrastructure automation tools, IaC maturity models, industry frameworks, and operational best practices. All sources have been cross-referenced and validated for accuracy.

Sources are organized into five categories: (1) Tool Documentation and Architecture -- official documentation for Ansible, Terraform, Chef, Puppet, and SaltStack; (2) IaC Maturity Models -- frameworks from JISEM, Ken Muse, Gomboc, Gary Stafford, and AWS; (3) Industry Frameworks -- CNCF autonomous infrastructure vision, GitOps principles, SRE practices, DevSecOps models; (4) Quantitative Research -- ITIC, Splunk, Cisco, IBM/NeuralWired studies on automation ROI; (5) Policy-as-Code -- OPA, Sentinel, and Kyverno documentation and best practices.

Key references include: JISEM Five-Stage IaC Maturity Model (December 2025), validated across finance, telecommunications, and government sectors; Ken Muse Five-Level IaC Maturity Model (January 2025) defining Initial through Optimizing levels; Gomboc IaC Maturity Curve (2025) from Ad-Hoc to Self-Correcting; CNCF Autonomous Infrastructure Vision (October 2025); ITIC Hourly Cost of Downtime Study establishing $300K+ per hour for mid-size enterprises; IBM/NeuralWired AIOps ROI Data (2026) demonstrating 300% ROI at Level 4 maturity; Cisco Networking Research (2025) finding 77% of organizations experienced major outages; Red Hat Ansible Documentation and Ansible Automation Platform Architecture Guide; HashiCorp Terraform Documentation and Terraform Cloud Architecture; Puppet Puppet Enterprise Documentation; Chef Chef Infra Documentation; SaltStack Salt Documentation.

The sources demonstrate strong convergence in the infrastructure automation domain around GitOps workflows, Policy-as-Code enforcement, platform engineering integration, and AI-assisted automation. Multiple independent maturity models align on similar progression stages (manual, codified, converged, governed, autonomous), providing cross-validation for the Asset Governance alpha states. The quantitative research consistently shows significant ROI from automation investment, with error reduction of 60-75%, MTTR improvements of 40-87%, and projected 300% ROI within 18 months at advanced maturity levels.

Extension practices built on Infrastructure Automation Essentials should reference tool-specific documentation as primary sources. Future baseline revisions should incorporate emerging research on AI-driven infrastructure autonomy, particularly as the CNCF autonomous infrastructure vision materializes. Annual review of the Asset Governance maturity model against industry maturity data is recommended to ensure continued alignment with organizational realities.
